items.prompt: Why can a crocodile's jaws bite down with tremendous force, yet a person can hold the same jaws shut with just their hands?

options.label: The muscles that close the jaw are huge, but the muscles that open it are comparatively weak
options.feedback: Nearly all of a crocodile's jaw muscle is devoted to slamming the mouth shut with great force, while the much smaller muscles that open it again produce comparatively little force.

options.label: The jaw locks shut automatically once it closes around anything
options.feedback: No locking mechanism is involved; the imbalance comes from how the muscle power is distributed between closing and opening, not from any latch.

options.label: The teeth are too sharp to allow the jaw to reopen safely
options.feedback: Tooth sharpness has nothing to do with how easily the jaw reopens; the real explanation lies in the difference in muscle strength for closing versus opening.

options.label: The jaw muscles tire out completely the instant they close
options.feedback: The closing muscles do not go weak the moment they succeed; it is the separate, much smaller opening muscles that were always comparatively weak to begin with.

items.ok_line: Enormous power to close, very little to open.
items.ko_line: Nothing locks or dulls here; think about how the muscle strength is split between closing and opening.
items.exp_title: Strength built in one direction only
items.exp_text: A crocodile's skull is dominated by massive muscles whose entire job is slamming the jaws shut, giving the bite tremendous crushing force once prey is caught. The muscles responsible for the opposite motion, pulling the jaws back open, are comparatively small and weak, since a crocodile has little evolutionary need for a powerful opening stroke. Because of this imbalance, holding the jaws closed with steady outside pressure takes far less strength than escaping the grip of a jaw that is already closing on something.

items.prompt: How can a crocodile lie almost entirely hidden underwater while still watching for prey?

options.label: It relies on hearing alone while its whole head stays submerged
options.feedback: A submerged head with ears underwater is not how a crocodile watches for prey this way; the key feature is that certain sense organs stay above the surface, not that hearing replaces sight.

options.label: Its skin changes color to match the surface of the water
options.feedback: No color-matching happens here; concealment comes from how little of the body needs to break the surface at all, not from blending in visually.

options.label: Its eyes, ears and nostrils sit raised on top of its skull, so only a sliver breaks the surface
options.feedback: Positioned high on the skull rather than on the sides of the head, the eyes, ears and nostrils can all stay just above the waterline while the entire rest of the body remains submerged and hidden.

options.label: It floats using a pocket of air trapped under its lower jaw
options.feedback: No air pocket under the jaw is involved; what keeps the crocodile so well hidden is simply the placement of its sensory organs on top of the skull.

items.ok_line: Only the very top of the skull needs to break the surface.
items.ko_line: This is about where the sense organs sit on the skull, not about color, hearing alone, or a trapped air pocket.
items.exp_title: Sense organs raised to the very top
items.exp_text: A crocodile's eyes, ears and nostrils are all positioned on raised points at the very top of its skull, rather than spread around the sides of the head the way they are in many other animals. This arrangement means the crocodile can submerge nearly its entire body, keeping only these small raised points above the waterline, while still being able to see, hear and breathe normally. To any prey approaching the water's edge, there is little more visible than a few small ripples and a pair of eyes.

items.prompt: How does a crocodile protect and still use its eyes while swimming underwater?

options.label: It relies entirely on the heat-sensing pits on its jaw instead of its eyes
options.feedback: Crocodiles do not have the heat-sensing pits that some snakes use; underwater, they still rely on their eyes, just protected in a particular way.

options.label: A clear inner eyelid closes over the eye like a built-in pair of goggles
options.feedback: A translucent third eyelid, called a nictitating membrane, slides across each eye and stays closed while swimming, shielding it from the water while still letting enough light through to see.

options.label: It simply closes both eyes completely until it resurfaces
options.feedback: Fully shutting the eyes would leave the crocodile unable to see anything at all underwater; the actual solution keeps some vision available even while submerged.

options.label: A layer of natural oil coats the eyes and repels the water
options.feedback: No oily coating covers the eyes for this purpose; the protection instead comes from a separate transparent membrane that closes over each eye.

items.ok_line: A clear third eyelid works like built-in underwater goggles.
items.ko_line: The eyes are neither fully shut nor coated in oil; think about a membrane that could stay clear enough to see through.
items.exp_text: In addition to its two ordinary eyelids, a crocodile has a third, translucent eyelid called a nictitating membrane, which can slide sideways across the whole eye. While swimming or diving, this membrane stays drawn across the eye, shielding it from the water and any debris while still allowing enough light through for the crocodile to see reasonably well. Once back at the surface, the membrane retracts again, leaving the eye fully exposed as before.

items.prompt: How does a crocodile keep water out of its throat while opening its jaws underwater to grip prey?

options.label: A flap of tissue at the back of the mouth seals off the throat from the airway
options.feedback: Called a palatal valve, this flap presses shut against the back of the throat, sealing the passage to the lungs and stomach so the mouth can open underwater without water flooding in past it.

options.label: It holds its breath so tightly that no water can be drawn in
options.feedback: Holding the breath alone would not stop water from simply flowing into an open mouth; a physical seal further back in the throat is what actually blocks it.

options.label: Its nostrils close automatically, sealing off the whole head
options.feedback: Closing the nostrils affects breathing through the nose, not water entering through an open mouth; the seal that matters here sits at the back of the throat.

options.label: Thick mucus coats the throat and repels incoming water
options.feedback: No mucus barrier is involved; the actual mechanism is a solid flap of tissue that physically closes off the throat passage.

items.ok_line: A flap at the back of the throat seals it off from the mouth.
items.ko_line: Nothing about held breath, closed nostrils, or mucus explains this; think about a physical seal further back in the mouth.
items.exp_title: A valve that seals the throat shut
items.exp_text: At the back of a crocodile's mouth sits a flap of tissue called a palatal valve, which presses upward to seal off the passage leading to the throat, lungs and stomach. This seal lets the crocodile open its jaws wide underwater to seize and hold onto prey without water flooding down into its airway or stomach in the process. Only once the valve relaxes again, typically once the head is back above the surface, does that passage reopen.

items.prompt: How does the "death roll" help a crocodile tear apart prey too large to swallow whole?

options.label: It shakes the prey rapidly side to side while staying still itself
options.feedback: The crocodile's own body is what spins in this maneuver, not merely the prey being shaken while the crocodile stays fixed in place.

options.label: It drags the prey along the riverbed to wear it down by friction
options.feedback: Dragging along a surface is not the mechanism here; the tearing force comes from the crocodile's own body rotating rapidly, not from scraping against the riverbed.

options.label: It repeatedly slams the prey against the water's surface
options.feedback: Slamming against the surface plays no part in this particular maneuver; the twisting motion of the crocodile's own body is what generates the tearing force.

options.label: It spins its whole body rapidly around its own long axis while its jaws stay locked on
options.feedback: With its teeth clamped onto a chunk of flesh, the crocodile rolls its entire body around its own length at speed, and since it cannot chew, this twisting force is what tears a manageable piece free.

items.ok_line: The crocodile's own body does the spinning, not the prey.
items.ko_line: Nothing about dragging or slamming explains this; think about what part of the crocodile actually rotates.
items.exp_title: Tearing by twisting its own body
items.exp_text: Once a crocodile's jaws are firmly clamped onto a piece of prey too large to swallow whole, it spins its entire body rapidly around its own long axis while keeping its bite locked in place. Because the prey's flesh cannot rotate along with the crocodile's twisting body, the strain quickly tears a manageable chunk free where the two forces pull against each other. This rolling motion stands in for the chewing that a crocodile's jaws are not built to do at all.

items.prompt: Why can't a crocodile chew the food it catches?

options.label: Its jaw can only move up and down, never side to side or in a grinding motion
options.feedback: The jaw's straight up-and-down motion is part of the picture, but the deeper reason chewing does not happen lies in the shape of the teeth themselves.

options.label: It has far too few teeth to grind anything effectively
options.feedback: A crocodile actually has a great many teeth lining its jaws; the issue is not how many there are but what shape each one takes.

options.label: Its teeth are pointed for gripping and puncturing, not flat for grinding
options.feedback: Built as sharp, conical points rather than flat-topped grinding surfaces, a crocodile's teeth are suited to seizing and holding prey firmly, not to crushing or chewing it into smaller pieces.

options.label: Its jaw muscles are too weak to sustain a repeated chewing motion
options.feedback: The jaw-closing muscles are anything but weak; the reason chewing does not happen is the shape of the teeth themselves, not a lack of muscle strength.

items.ok_line: Pointed teeth grip and puncture; they were never built to grind.
items.ko_line: This is about the shape of the teeth, not the number of them or the strength of the jaw muscles.
items.exp_title: Teeth built for gripping, not grinding
items.exp_text: A crocodile's teeth are simple, sharp cones, each one shaped for stabbing into flesh and holding it firmly rather than for crushing or grinding it the way a flat-topped molar would. Because none of its teeth offer a grinding surface, closing the jaws on food only punctures and grips it, and no amount of biting down will break it into smaller pieces the way chewing does. Instead, a crocodile is limited to tearing off pieces it can swallow whole, or to gulping down prey small enough to pass entirely.

items.prompt: How does a crocodile manage to digest bones and tough prey it swallows whole?

options.label: It has an extra stomach chamber devoted purely to storage, with no digestion
options.feedback: There is no purely storage-only stomach chamber involved; digestion itself is handled by an unusually powerful combination inside a single stomach.

options.label: It swallows stones that grind food, combined with extremely strong stomach acid
options.feedback: Stones deliberately swallowed and kept in the stomach act like millstones, physically grinding down tough material, while stomach acid far stronger than a human's works chemically to break the rest down, including bone.

options.label: It regurgitates and re-swallows meals several times before digesting them
options.feedback: Repeated regurgitation is not the mechanism at work; digestion instead relies on physically grinding tough material and on unusually powerful stomach acid.

options.label: Bacteria in its mouth pre-digest the meal before it is ever swallowed
options.feedback: No meaningful pre-digestion happens in the mouth; the heavy work of breaking down bone and tough tissue happens afterward, inside the stomach itself.

items.ok_line: Swallowed stones grind the food, and strong acid dissolves the rest.
items.ko_line: No extra storage chamber or mouth bacteria is involved; think about what happens physically and chemically inside the stomach.
items.exp_title: A stomach built to grind and dissolve
items.exp_text: A crocodile deliberately swallows stones that settle and stay in its stomach, where they act much like millstones, physically grinding tough material such as bone and shell as the stomach muscles churn. Alongside this, its stomach produces acid strong enough to dissolve even hard material chemically, far more concentrated than the digestive acid of many other animals. Between the physical grinding of the stones and the strength of the acid, a crocodile can break down prey that would pass through most other digestive systems largely intact.

items.prompt: How does a crocodile detect the faintest ripple of movement in water even in complete darkness?

options.label: Tiny pressure-sensitive domes scattered over its jaws pick up the slightest ripple
options.feedback: Dotted across the skin of the jaws, these small dome-shaped sensory organs respond to the faintest changes in water pressure, letting a crocodile detect movement nearby without needing to see or hear it.

options.label: Its ears are specially tuned to detect underwater sound at long range
options.feedback: Sound detection through the ears is a separate sense; the extremely fine detection of ripples right at the surface of the water relies on a different set of sensory organs entirely, located on the jaws.

options.label: Its nostrils can smell chemical traces left behind by movement in the water
options.feedback: Smell works through chemical traces, not through physical ripples; picking up the sheer motion of water depends instead on pressure-sensitive organs on the skin.

options.label: Whiskers similar to a cat's grow along the sides of its snout
options.feedback: A crocodile has no whiskers of this kind; what it has instead are small dome-shaped organs embedded directly in the skin along its jaws.

items.ok_line: Tiny pressure sensors on the jaws pick up the faintest ripple.
items.ko_line: This is not about ears, nose, or whiskers; think about sensors built directly into the skin of the jaws.
items.exp_title: Skin that senses the water itself
items.exp_text: Small dome-shaped structures are scattered across the skin covering a crocodile's jaws, each one packed with nerve endings sensitive to the tiniest changes in pressure moving through the water. Even a very faint ripple, such as one made by a fish swimming nearby in total darkness, disturbs the water enough for these domes to register it and pass the signal on. This sense works whether or not the crocodile can see or hear anything at all, letting it strike accurately toward a target it has never laid eyes on.

items.prompt: How does a mother crocodile know when it is time to help her hatchlings dig their way out of the underground nest?

options.label: She digs up the nest automatically after a fixed number of days pass
options.feedback: The timing is not set by counting days on a schedule; it depends instead on a signal the hatchlings themselves send once they are ready.

options.label: The hatchlings make chirping sounds inside their eggs that she can hear
options.feedback: Once ready to hatch, the young inside their eggs begin to call out, and these sounds carry up through the soil well enough for the waiting mother to hear and respond by digging the nest open.

options.label: She smells a chemical change in the soil covering the nest
options.feedback: No chemical change in the soil is what triggers her; the signal that reaches her is a sound made by the hatchlings themselves, not a scent.

options.label: She feels ground vibrations produced by the hatchlings pushing against the eggshell
options.feedback: It is the sound the hatchlings make, not vibration felt through the ground, that alerts a waiting mother to begin digging.

items.ok_line: The hatchlings' own calls, heard through the soil, bring her digging.
items.ko_line: This is not about a fixed schedule, a smell, or vibration; think about a sound the hatchlings themselves could make.
items.exp_title: Calls that reach through the soil
items.exp_text: Shortly before hatching, the young crocodiles inside their eggs begin making chirping or grunting sounds, still fully enclosed within both the shell and the soil covering the nest. A mother crocodile that has been guarding the nest area can hear these calls well enough through the ground to recognize that hatching has begun. Responding to the sound, she digs down to uncover the nest and often carries newly hatched young gently in her mouth down to the water.

items.prompt: How does a crocodile stay so motionless in the water while waiting for prey to come near, without needing to keep swimming?

options.label: It anchors itself to the riverbed using its claws
options.feedback: No anchoring with claws is involved; staying still and staying afloat come from a separate ability related to buoyancy, not from gripping the bottom.

options.label: It rests its full weight on submerged rocks or logs
options.feedback: A crocodile does not need to rest on a submerged surface to stay still; it can hold a steady position out in open water using its own control over buoyancy.

options.label: It ties its tail around underwater plants to hold its position
options.feedback: No tying or gripping of plants is involved; the stillness comes from an internal ability to adjust how the body floats, not from anchoring to anything external.

options.label: It shifts its lungs and repositions internal organs to fine-tune its buoyancy
options.feedback: By adjusting the position of its lungs and other organs within the body cavity, a crocodile can fine-tune exactly how it floats, letting it hang almost motionless at a chosen depth without paddling to hold position.

items.ok_line: Shifting internal organs fine-tunes exactly how the body floats.
items.ko_line: No anchoring to the riverbed, rocks, or plants is involved; think about something the crocodile can adjust inside its own body.
items.exp_text: A crocodile can shift the position of its lungs and other organs within its body cavity, moving its center of buoyancy without needing to move its limbs at all. This lets it settle at a chosen depth and hold almost perfectly still in the water, floating with only its eyes and nostrils above the surface for as long as it needs to wait. Because this control comes from inside the body rather than from paddling or gripping something external, a waiting crocodile can stay motionless for a very long stretch without tiring.
